intro: Activation rate is the share of new users who reach whatever first meaningful action a product has defined as "activated." Enter activated users and installs (or signups) to get the rate.

sections.heading: How Activation Rate is calculated
sections.body: Activation Rate = Activated Users ÷ Installs (or signups) — [the same activated-over-total shape Geckoboard uses to define the metric](https://www.geckoboard.com/best-practice/kpi-examples/activation-rate/). The formula is simple; what varies is what counts as "activated," which the formula itself doesn't define.

sections.heading: Worked example
sections.body: 3,200 ÷ 8,000 = 40.00%. Whether that's a strong result depends entirely on what "activated" was defined to mean here — reaching a first meaningful action is a very different bar than simply opening the app once.

sections.heading: "Activated" is a product-defined event, not a universal one
sections.body: There's no single activation event that applies across every product. [A social app might track the share of users who add their first friend; a music app might track who builds a first playlist](https://www.geckoboard.com/best-practice/kpi-examples/activation-rate/) — the common thread is that the event should raise the odds a user sticks around, not that it's the same event everywhere. This calculator computes whatever activation event you enter into it; it doesn't supply one. Reporting an activation rate without naming the underlying event strips out the one piece of context that makes the number meaningful at all.

sections.heading: Activation Rate vs. Conversion Rate
sections.body: Both are "share of X that did Y" ratios, but they're built for different moments. [Conversion Rate](/calculators/cr) tracks a specific transaction — a visitor becoming a customer, an opportunity becoming a sale — measured against opportunities or visitors as the denominator. Activation Rate tracks a product-usage milestone specifically tied to onboarding, measured against installs or signups. A high-converting product can still have weak activation if new users buy in but never reach the point where the product clicks for them, and the reverse: strong activation doesn't guarantee the purchase or signup conversion that got them there in the first place.

sections.heading: Common mistakes
items: Reporting activation rate without naming the specific event counted as "activated." The number is meaningless on its own without that context, since the same rate can describe very different bars.
Assuming activated users can exceed installs. A user activating twice, or being counted incorrectly across install cohorts, produces a rate that doesn't describe any real installed base.

Comparing activation rate across products, or across your own product's different activation definitions, as if the numbers describe the same milestone. They don't unless the underlying event is identical.
Setting the activation bar so low it's reached passively (e.g. opening the app once) that it stops correlating with the retention behavior activation is meant to predict in the first place.

faq.a: Activation rate is the percentage of new users who reach a defined first meaningful action, calculated as activated users divided by installs or signups. What counts as "activated" is set by the product, not by a universal standard — a social app might define it as adding a first friend, while a music app might define it as building a first playlist. The common requirement across products is that the event should meaningfully raise the odds a user sticks around, not just that it's easy to hit. Reporting activation rate always requires naming the specific event it's measuring, since the number means nothing without that context.

faq.q: How do you calculate Activation Rate?
faq.a: Divide activated users by installs (or signups): Activation Rate = Activated Users ÷ Installs. A cohort of 8,000 new installs with 3,200 reaching the activation event has an activation rate of 3,200 ÷ 8,000 = 40.00%. Both numbers need to describe the same cohort and measurement window — activated users from a broader time range than the installs they're divided by will overstate the rate. The activation event itself also needs to stay fixed between calculations; comparing a rate computed against one definition to a rate computed against another isn't a real comparison, even if both are labeled "activation rate."

faq.q: Who decides what counts as an activation event?
faq.a: The product team does, based on what data actually correlates with users sticking around. There's no industry-standard activation event that applies across every product — what counts for a social app (adding a first friend) looks nothing like what counts for a productivity tool (completing a first project) or an e-commerce app (finishing a first purchase). A well-chosen activation event is one that's been shown to predict retention, not simply the easiest action to track. Because the definition varies this much, any activation rate reported without stating the underlying event is missing the context needed to interpret it. Teams often revisit the definition as they gather more retention data, tightening or loosening the bar as they learn what actually predicts a user sticking around.

faq.q: How is Activation Rate different from Conversion Rate?
faq.a: Conversion Rate tracks a specific transaction — a visitor becoming a customer, an opportunity becoming a sale — with visitors or opportunities as the denominator. Activation Rate tracks a product-usage milestone tied specifically to onboarding, measured against installs or signups instead. A product can convert well (people sign up or buy) while activating poorly (few of them ever reach the point where the product delivers value), and the reverse is also possible. The two metrics measure genuinely different moments in the user journey, even though both are structured as a share of one group that did something. Tracking both side by side is often more useful than either alone, since a gap between them usually points to a specific stage of the journey worth investigating.

faq.q: What is a good Activation Rate?
faq.a: There's no universal good activation rate — it depends entirely on how strict the activation event is defined, the product category, and the acquisition channel bringing users in, all of which shift the number before product quality even enters the picture. A demanding activation bar (completing a multi-step setup) will naturally post a lower rate than a lenient one (opening the app once), without either definition being wrong. The more useful comparison is your own product's activation rate over time, using the same event definition, since that holds the bar constant and actually reflects whether onboarding improved. Published industry averages exist for specific product categories, but applying one to a product with a differently defined activation event compares two unlike things.
